claims.text: The initial FeNiCrCoCu coating has an ordered FCC lattice structure.
At high temperature, the coating transitions locally from crystalline FCC order to an amorphous phase at the contact interface.
Above 900 K, thermal activation causes rapid stacking-fault annihilation.
Stacking-fault annihilation causes dislocation starvation.
Dislocation starvation forces the lattice into a high-energy state.
The dislocation-starved high-energy lattice relaxes through rapid interfacial amorphization.
The resulting amorphous interfacial layer has low shear strength.
Viscous-like flow of the low-shear-strength amorphous layer causes a friction-coefficient spike.
The amorphous layer cannot support load effectively, causing loss of wear resistance.
The friction coefficient increases sharply at 900 K and 1200 K.
Hardness and wear resistance decrease precipitously at 900 K and 1200 K.
High-temperature degradation is correlated with an increase in non-FCC atomic coordination in the contact zone.
High-temperature degradation is correlated with a decrease in total dislocation line length in the contact zone.
At 300 K and 600 K, dislocation density is maintained or only slightly reduced.
Amorphization does not occur at 300 K or 600 K.
The 300 K and 600 K states retain stable hardness and lower friction.
At lower strain rates or in polycrystalline variants, grain-boundary sliding may dominate and the proposed mechanism may not apply.
Introducing stable HCP stacking faults or dislocation loops will inhibit dislocation starvation and subsequent amorphization.
Inhibiting dislocation starvation with pre-existing defects should suppress the friction spike and preserve wear resistance at 900 K.

Persistence of friction and wear degradation despite retained HCP defects and dislocations would favor direct thermal softening or lattice instability over the proposed starvation-amorphization sequence.

contradictions.description: The amorphous layer is described as low in shear strength and as facilitating sliding, yet that same property is said to cause a friction-coefficient spike. Without an additional dissipative or adhesive mechanism, facilitated low-shear sliding would ordinarily imply reduced rather than increased friction.
The proposed mechanism is stated to operate 'above 900 K' or at temperatures '>900 K,' while the predicted outcome explicitly includes onset at exactly 900 K.
